title: Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)

paper.title: Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)
paper.abstract:
Abstract Data selection is critical for training large language models on
massive and heterogeneous corpora. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection offers a principled alternative to heuristic scoring by learning data
weights from a target validation objective, but existing methods face a
trade-off between fine-grained valuation and transferability to unseen data.
A natural solution is to replace per-sample weights with a selection network.
However, we find that directly incorporating such a network into existing MTS
objectives leads to unstable optimization and poor generalization, caused by
weight suppression and persistent reliance on easy-to-learn features. To
address these issues, we propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS), a scalable data-selection
framework built on a Pointwise Value Matching objective (PVM). Experiments on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning demonstrate
strong transfer across datasets, from subsets to full corpora, and from
smaller to larger models.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The performance of modern AI systems is fundamentally shaped by the training data ( Zha et al., 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2024 ; Zha et al., 2023 ; Whang et al., 2023 ) . For large language models (LLMs), scaling requires assembling massive corpora from heterogeneous sources ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Weber et al., 2024 ; Langlais et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2024a ) , which often introduces redundant and low-quality examples. Training data selection is hence an important component of LLM training. Many existing methods rank training examples by manually designed scores, such as entropy ( Li et al., 2026 ) , instruction-following difficulty ( Li et al., 2024b ) , reducible training loss ( Mindermann et al., 2022 ) , and distance to target domain ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) , to name a few. These scoring rules lack the ability to dynamically adapt to new scenarios. Though each captures a potentially useful signal, it remains an open question how these scores may be combined to create more powerful ranking mechanisms. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection (MTS) ( Shen et al., 2025a ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Calian et al., 2026 ) provides a principled alternative, where the values of training data are learned directly from their effects on the validation loss ℒ val \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}} . Let 𝜽 \bm{\theta} denote the LLM parameters, w i > 0 w_{i}>0 be the learnable weight for the loss of the i i -th training data point, ℓ i ​ ( 𝜽 ) \ell_{i}(\bm{\theta}) , and the vector 𝒘 = ( w i ) i \bm{w}=(w_{i})_{i} contain all w i w_{i} as components. MTS formulates data weighting as the following bilevel optimization problem: 𝐰 ∗ = arg ⁡ min 𝐰 ​ ℒ val ​ ( 𝜽 ∗ ​ ( 𝐰 ) ) , s. t. 𝜽 ∗ ​ ( 𝐰 ) = arg ⁡ min 𝜽 | 𝒘 | ∑ i 1 − 1 ⁡ w i ​ ℓ i ​ ( 𝜽 ) . \mathbf{w}^{*}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\bigl(\bm{\theta}^{*}(\mathbf{w})\bigr),\qquad\text{s. t.}\quad\bm{\theta}^{*}(\mathbf{w})=\arg\min_{\bm{\theta}}\|\bm{w}\|_{1}^{-1}\sum_{i}w_{i}\ell_{i}(\bm{\theta}). (1) This framework allows automatic identification of effective training data, which lead the model to generalize to the validation data. Nevertheless, MTS in practice runs into two obstacles; the first is scalability. Computing the exact hypergradient ∇ 𝒘 ℒ val ​ ( 𝜽 ∗ ​ ( 𝐰 ) ) \nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\bm{\theta}^{*}(\mathbf{w})) by unrolling the inner optimization is costly. Even unrolling one step and taking the finite-different approximation require three backward operations on 𝜽 \bm{\theta} for one gradient step on 𝒘 \bm{w} ( Du et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2019 ) , which is prohibitive expensive for large LLMs. Calian et al. (2026) manage to unroll 8 steps using 64 v5 TPUs, which is beyond the capability of most academic labs. With penalty-based reformulations ( Shen & Chen, 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025b ) , ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) reduces the number of backward calls to two, whereas SEAL ( Shen et al., 2025a ) reduces it further to one, but incurs discernible performance losses. The second challenge is generalization to unseen data. In the formulation of Ren et al. (2018) ; Shen et al. (2025a) , every data point receives a separate weight w i w_{i} , and no generalization is possible. An alternative approach ( Pan et al., 2025 ) is to assign a separate weight for each data domain (e.g., one dataset in a collection of multiple datasets), which provides generalization within each domain. However, this overlooks heterogeneity among data points in a single domain and cannot generalize to new data domains. One intuitively appealing idea is to train a meta-network that outputs w i w_{i} for every data point. If the meta-network can generalize to unseen data points, we would be able to train on a small dataset and perform data selection on a much larger dataset, which would also substantially improve efficiency and scalability. Though the meta-network approach has been used by Shu et al. (2019) ; Du et al. (2026) ; Calian et al. (2026) , no such generalization has been reported, not even for the extraordinarily large-scale experiments of Calian et al. (2026) . Perhaps unsurprisingly, our experiments find simplistic training of the meta-network leads to unstable optimization (Figure 2 ) and poor generalization (Table 1 and 3 ). Given the massive success of deep learning, the failure of the meta-network to generalize to unseen data is especially perplexing. Our analysis traces the failure to two properties of the training loss. First, as training progresses, most predicted data weights are suppressed toward zero. As a result, over time, the meta-network loses the ability to distinguish useful training data from harmful training data. Second, the loss causes the network to exclusively learn easy features and ignores hard feature, so the network becomes susceptible to shortcut learning. To improve the scalability and generalization of MTS, we propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS). At its core, TESS simplifies ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and introduces a simple mean squared error objective, which we call Pointwise Value Matching (PVM). TESS constructs sample-level pseudo-labels that capture the utility of training data points and uses these values as supervision for the data-selecting meta-network. Compared to the existing loss, the PVM loss is less focused on easy features, which curbs shortcut learning and promotes generalization. Further, TESS removes the requirement of ScaleBiO to simultaneously train two LLMs with the meta-network, cutting peak memory footprint by more than 20%. Experiments on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning demonstrate substantially improved generalization of TESS across three settings: cross-dataset transfer, small-to-large model transfer, and subset-to-full-corpus transfer. Our contributions can be summarized as: • We identify and theoretically analyze two limitations of applying the existing MTS training objective to a shared selection network: competitive weight suppression that undermines the identification of high-quality training data, and persistent preference for easy-to-learn features that can encourage shortcut learning. • We propose TESS, a transferable data-selection framework that constructs sample-level pseudo-labels and uses them as supervision to learn a data selection network generalizable to unseen data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that demonstrates generalization to unseen data in MTS.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Meta-Learning Data Selection for LLMs. Scaling meta-learning data selection to LLMs requires efficiency in face of both huge parameter counts ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and dataset sizes ( Xie et al., 2023b ) . Traditional data selection methods ( Ren et al., 2018 ; Shu et al., 2019 ) differentiate through model updates to compute the hypergradient, which incurs large time and space complexity for large models. ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and SEAL ( Shen et al., 2025a ) focus on scaling to model parameter counts. If data selection can be trained on a small dataset and generalize to unseen data, it would also significantly improve scalability to large datasets. However, such generalization remains a difficult challenge. In terms of generalization, existing approaches can be broadly grouped into sample-level, domain-level, and meta-network methods. Example-level methods ( Xie et al., 2023b ; Xia et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025a ; Calian et al., 2026 ) learn one weight for each training data point, thereby offering no generalization to new data points. Domain-level methods ( Xie et al., 2023a ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2026 ) partition the training data into domains and assign one data weight to each domain. Chameleon ( Xie et al., 2025 ) and Data Mixing Agent ( Yang et al., 2026 ) further introduce a shared domain taxonomy that enables limited weight sharing among data domains. However, domain-level weights are too coarse to capture the crucial differences in data quality and content within each domain ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Meta-network methods ( Shu et al., 2019 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Calian et al., 2026 ) train a meta-network to output the weight for each data point directly. In theory, this should allow generalization to new data points; in practice, no generalization has been reported. Notably, DataRater ( Calian et al., 2026 ) trains a separate scorer for each dataset, suggesting generalization across dataset is challenging even when the network are trained with a huge amount of data. With this paper, we analyze the reasons behind the challenge mathematically and offer a simple, practical, and high-performance solution. Shortcut Learning. Shortcut learning occurs when models rely on easy features that are strongly predictive of training labels but whose correlations weaken or reverse under distribution shifts, impairing out-of-distribution generalization ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ; Shah et al., 2020 ) . Prior work distinguishes predictivity , how reliably a feature predicts training labels, from availability , how easily it can be extracted ( Hermann et al., 2024 ) . Scimeca et al. (2021) find that solutions favoring easy-to-learn cues tend to lie in flatter minima and are more abundant in parameter space, while Qiu et al. (2024) show that simpler or more strongly correlated spurious features can slow core-feature learning. We investigate these dynamics in data selection networks. We show that the ScaleBiO loss continues to reinforce easy-to-learn features that are susceptible to shortcut learning, while our proposed PVM promotes the learning of harder and more transferable features.

sections.heading: 4 Why the ScaleBiO Loss Performs Poorly
sections.text: We next examine why optimizing with the ScaleBiO objective can fail to produce a transferable meta-network. We identify two properties of the ScaleBiO objective: competitive weight suppression, which weakens sample discrimination, and a persistent preference for easy-to-learn features, which can encourage shortcut learning.

As training progresses, however, its outputs become less discriminative. This creates a strange phenomenon that more training leads to worsened data selection even on the training set itself. Empirical verification. Figure 1 illustrates this behavior through a numerical simulation. The weight w 1 w_{1} , associated with the largest pseudo-label, becomes dominant, while the remaining weights reach the lower bound. Notably, w 4 w_{4} initially increases but later decreases. Between t = 0.4 t=0.4 and t = 0.6 t=0.6 , the weights can separate good data with the highest pseudo-labels, but this period is transient. Some data selection can be achieved by carefully tuning early stopping (consistent with Figure 9 of Calian et al. (2026) ) but it requires significant trial and error. To verify these dynamics, we construct a controlled dataset by mixing GSM8K and unsafe examples at a 2 : 1 2{:}1 ratio, together with a disjoint unseen set of the same composition. This way, we know exactly what data points are unsafe and should be discarded. We rank examples by predicted weights and evaluate how accurately the bottom one-third identifies unsafe examples on both seen and unseen data. Experimental details are provided in Appendix E . Figure 2 compares ScaleBiO with ℒ ϕ SBO \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{SBO}}} , TESS with ℒ ϕ SBO \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{SBO}}} , and TESS with ℒ ϕ PVM \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{PVM}}} . Figure 2: Training dynamics of ScaleBiO and TESS under different meta-network objectives. With SBO loss, most predicted weights shrink toward zero as accuracy declines. In contrast, PVM loss maintains nonvanishing weight quantiles and high accuracy. Under ℒ ϕ SBO \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{SBO}}} , the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile of the predicted weights progressively approach zero, consistent with the competitive suppression analyzed above. The maximum weight initially increases but later decreases. This is expected because a shared selection network typically produces smoother outputs than a one-hot vector ( Ma & Ying, 2021 ) , causing even dominant weights to decrease as most outputs are suppressed. Weight suppression accompanies declining discrimination. For ScaleBiO, seen and unseen accuracy first improve but eventually fall to around 60 % 60\% . TESS with the same ℒ ϕ SBO \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{SBO}}} exhibits a similar long-term decline, although it improves immediately at the beginning of training. We attribute this early difference to the quality of the supervision signal: ScaleBiO updates the meta-network while the two LLMs are still being optimized, whereas TESS computes loss gaps from well-trained, fixed LLMs. In contrast, TESS with ℒ ϕ PVM \smash{\mathcal{L}_{\bm{\phi}}^{\mathrm{PVM}}} maintains stable, nonvanishing weight quantiles and reaches 98.58 % 98.58\% seen accuracy and 97.96 % 97.96\% unseen accuracy.

We use Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ; Peng et al., 2023 ) and Dolly ( Conover et al., 2023 ) as candidate pools 𝒟 pool \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pool}} . The validation set from He et al. We use LlamaGuard 3 ( Llama Team, 2024 ) as the classifier to compute attack success rate (ASR) from generated responses; higher ASR indicates more effective harmful-data selection. sections.heading: 5.2 Targeted Instruction Tuning
sections.text: We evaluate if TESS trained on a small subset can generalize to the full instruction tuning corpus. GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) and Codex ( Chen et al., 2021 ) are the target tasks. The heuristic methods, LESS ( Xia et al., 2024 ) and RDS+ ( Ivison et al., 2025 ) , rank candidate examples using predefined measures of relevance to the target validation set. All four learnable baselines are trained on the same 50K subset. SEAL w and SBO w are restricted to select from their training set. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced TESS, a transferable data-selection framework that learns a selector from sample-level pseudo-labels. We identify weight suppression and easy-feature preference of ScaleBiO objective and address them with PVM. TESS shows strong transfer across datasets, corpus scales, and model sizes.

sections.heading: D.1 Datasets
sections.text: For LLM safety, we use Alpaca and Dolly as training datasets and evaluate on DirectHarm4, HarmBench, and HEx-PHI: • Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ; Peng et al., 2023 ) contains 52,002 instruction–response pairs covering diverse instruction-following tasks. • Dolly ( Conover et al., 2023 ) contains 15,011 human-written instruction–response pairs covering tasks such as question answering, summarization, and creative writing. • DirectHarm4 (DH4) ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) contains 400 harmful instructions, with 100 examples in each of four categories: malware, drugs, phishing, and disinformation. • HarmBench (HB) ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) evaluates harmful behavior generation. Its text-only portion contains 400 behaviors across standard, contextual, and copyright-related categories. • HEx-PHI (HEx) ( Qi et al., 2024 ) evaluates responses to instructions spanning prohibited-use categories. Its original release contains 330 instructions, with 30 examples in each of 11 categories: illegal activity, child abuse content, hate/harassment/violence, malware, physical harm, economic harm, fraud/deception, adult content, political campaigning, privacy violation, and tailored financial advice. For targeted instruction tuning, we use Tulu V2 as the candidate instruction corpus and evaluate data selection for GSM8K and CodeX: • Tulu V2 ( Ivison et al., 2025 ) is a multi-source instruction-tuning corpus; we use the approximately 200K-example version preprocessed by Nayak et al. (2026) , which excludes examples with no response tokens within the first 2,048 tokens. We train the meta-network on a random 50K subset and apply it to the full candidate pool. • GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) contains grade-school math problems with step-by-step solutions, comprising 7,473 training examples and 1,319 test examples. We hold out 1,000 examples from the training split as a shared validation set for all methods. • CodeX ( Chen et al., 2021 ) contains 164 Python function-completion problems with unit tests for evaluating functional correctness. Following Ivison et al. (2025) , we use 16 examples as the query set and the remaining 148 as the test set.

sections.text: meta-network learning. We train the two LLMs, 𝜽 U \bm{\theta}_{U} and 𝜽 W \bm{\theta}_{W} , using LISA ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , with learning rates in { 5 × 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 } \{5\times 10^{-5},10^{-4}\} for up to three epochs. We tune the training–validation trade-off coefficient α \alpha over { 0.01 , 0.1 , 1.0 } \{0.01,0.1,1.0\} . The meta-network is a three-layer MLP with a sigmoid output, optimized using AdamW with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Downstream fine-tuning for LLM safety. We apply LoRA to the query and key projections, W q W_{q} and W k W_{k} , in every Transformer layer, with rank r = 8 r=8 and α LoRA = 8 \alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}=8 . We train for three epochs with a batch size of 32, a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and a cosine learning rate schedule with a warmup ratio of 0.1. Downstream fine-tuning for targeted instruction tuning. We fully finetune Llama-2-7B on the selected examples for two epochs using AdamW with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} and a linear learning rate schedule. The maximum sequence length is 2,048 tokens.

sections.heading: D.3 Input Features to the Meta-Network
sections.text: Inspired by Du et al. (2026) , we construct sample-level features in both representation and gradient spaces. The representation embedding is the final-layer hidden state of the last token, and the gradient embedding is derived from the per-sample loss gradient. In each space, we compute the distances to each of the three nearest validation examples and to the mean validation embedding. We concatenate these eight distances with the sample’s loss and gradient norm to obtain a 10-dimensional feature vector. For LLM safety, we append a binary feature indicating whether the sample contains numbers or predefined keywords such as list , convert , and calculate . This feature is motivated by findings that some benign list-format and mathematical examples can degrade safety alignment after fine-tuning ( Chen et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: D.4 Evaluation Details
sections.text: LLM safety. For DH4, HB, and HEx, we generate model responses using greedy decoding (temperature 0). We classify each response as safe or unsafe using Llama Guard, also with greedy decoding. We report the attack success rate (ASR), defined as the percentage of evaluated responses classified as unsafe; lower is better. GSM8K. Following Ivison et al. (2025) , we use the eight chain-of-thought demonstrations as individual query examples for data selection, without prepending other demonstrations to each query. At evaluation time, we include all eight demonstrations in each test prompt and report exact-match accuracy of the extracted final numerical answers on the 1,319 test problems. CodeX. We sample code completions at a temperature of 0.8 and report pass@10 on the 148 held-out problems. This metric estimates the probability that at least one of ten sampled completions passes all unit tests for a problem.

sections.heading: Appendix G Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduced Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS), transferable data-selection framework that utilize sample-level pseudo-labels to learn a data selection network generalizable to unseen data. Our theoretical and empirical analyses identify competitive weight suppression and persistent easy-feature preference as limitations of the ScaleBiO meta-objective. To address these issues, we propose a new training objective PVM. Experiments demonstrate cross-dataset, subset-to-full-corpus, and small-to-large model transfer. Specifically, in terms of generalization, TESS outperforms the strongest learnable-weighting baselines by 22.75 22.75 and 3.99 3.99 points on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning, respectively.

Affiliation: College of Computing and Data Science Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University Affiliation: Singapore Email: boyang.li@ntu.edu.sg Abstract Data selection is critical for training large language models on massive and heterogeneous corpora. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection offers a principled alternative to heuristic scoring by learning data weights from a target validation objective, but existing methods face a trade-off between fine-grained valuation and transferability to unseen data. A natural solution is to replace per-sample weights with a selection network. However, we find that directly incorporating such a network into existing MTS objectives leads to unstable optimization and poor generalization, caused by weight suppression and persistent reliance on easy-to-learn features. To address these issues, we propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS), a scalable data-selection framework built on a Pointwise Value Matching objective (PVM). Experiments on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning demonstrate strong transfer across datasets, from subsets to full corpora, and from smaller to larger models. 1 Introduction The performance of modern AI systems is fundamentally shaped by the training data ( Zha et al., 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2024 ; Zha et al., 2023 ; Whang et al., 2023 ) . For large language models (LLMs), scaling requires assembling massive corpora from heterogeneous sources ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Weber et al., 2024 ; Langlais et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2024a ) , which often introduces redundant and low-quality examples. Training data selection is hence an important component of LLM training. Many existing methods rank training examples by manually designed scores, such as entropy ( Li et al., 2026 ) , instruction-following difficulty ( Li et al., 2024b ) , reducible training loss ( Mindermann et al., 2022 ) , and distance to target domain ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Min et al., 2026 ) , to name a few. These scoring rules lack the ability to dynamically adapt to new scenarios. Though each captures a potentially useful signal, it remains an open question how these scores may be combined to create more powerful ranking mechanisms. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection (MTS) ( Shen et al., 2025a ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Calian et al., 2026 ) provides a principled alternative, where the values of training data are learned directly from their effects on the validation loss ℒ val \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}} . Even unrolling one step and taking the finite-different approximation require three backward operations on 𝜽  m{	heta} for one gradient step on 𝒘  m{w} ( Du et al., 2026 ; Shu et al., 2019 ) , which is prohibitive expensive for large LLMs. Calian et al. (2026) manage to unroll 8 steps using 64 v5 TPUs, which is beyond the capability of most academic labs. With penalty-based reformulations ( Shen & Chen, 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Shen et al., 2025b ) , ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) reduces the number of backward calls to two, whereas SEAL ( Shen et al., 2025a ) reduces it further to one, but incurs discernible performance losses. The second challenge is generalization to unseen data. In the formulation of Ren et al. (2018) ; Shen et al. (2025a) , every data point receives a separate weight w i w_{i} , and no generalization is possible. An alternative approach ( Pan et al., 2025 ) is to assign a separate weight for each data domain (e.g., one dataset in a collection of multiple datasets), which provides generalization within each domain. However, this overlooks heterogeneity among data points in a single domain and cannot generalize to new data domains. One intuitively appealing idea is to train a meta-network that outputs w i w_{i} for every data point. If the meta-network can generalize to unseen data points, we would be able to train on a small dataset and perform data selection on a much larger dataset, which would also substantially improve efficiency and scalability. Though the meta-network approach has been used by Shu et al. (2019) ; Du et al. (2026) ; Calian et al. (2026) , no such generalization has been reported, not even for the extraordinarily large-scale experiments of Calian et al. (2026) . Perhaps unsurprisingly, our experiments find simplistic training of the meta-network leads to unstable optimization (Figure 2 ) and poor generalization (Table 1 and 3 ). Given the massive success of deep learning, the failure of the meta-network to generalize to unseen data is especially perplexing. Our analysis traces the failure to two properties of the training loss. First, as training progresses, most predicted data weights are suppressed toward zero. As a result, over time, the meta-network loses the ability to distinguish useful training data from harmful training data. Second, the loss causes the network to exclusively learn easy features and ignores hard feature, so the network becomes susceptible to shortcut learning. To improve the scalability and generalization of MTS, we propose Transferable Example Scoring and Selection (TESS). At its core, TESS simplifies ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and introduces a simple mean squared error objective, which we call Pointwise Value Matching (PVM). TESS constructs sample-level pseudo-labels that capture the utility of training data points and uses these values as supervision for the data-selecting meta-network. Compared to the existing loss, the PVM loss is less focused on easy features, which curbs shortcut learning and promotes generalization. Further, TESS removes the requirement of ScaleBiO to simultaneously train two LLMs with the meta-network, cutting peak memory footprint by more than 20%. Experiments on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning demonstrate substantially improved generalization of TESS across three settings: cross-dataset transfer, small-to-large model transfer, and subset-to-full-corpus transfer. Our contributions can be summarized as: • We identify and theoretically analyze two limitations of applying the existing MTS training objective to a shared selection network: competitive weight suppression that undermines the identification of high-quality training data, and persistent preference for easy-to-learn features that can encourage shortcut learning. • We propose TESS, a transferable data-selection framework that constructs sample-level pseudo-labels and uses them as supervision to learn a data selection network generalizable to unseen data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that demonstrates generalization to unseen data in MTS. 2 Related Work Meta-Learning Data Selection for LLMs. Scaling meta-learning data selection to LLMs requires efficiency in face of both huge parameter counts ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and dataset sizes ( Xie et al., 2023b ) . Traditional data selection methods ( Ren et al., 2018 ; Shu et al., 2019 ) differentiate through model updates to compute the hypergradient, which incurs large time and space complexity for large models. ScaleBiO ( Pan et al., 2025 ) and SEAL ( Shen et al., 2025a ) focus on scaling to model parameter counts. If data selection can be trained on a small dataset and generalize to unseen data, it would also significantly improve scalability to large datasets. However, such generalization remains a difficult challenge. In terms of generalization, existing approaches can be broadly grouped into sample-level, domain-level, and meta-network methods. Example-level methods ( Xie et al., 2023b ; Xia et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025a ; Calian et al., 2026 ) learn one weight for each training data point, thereby offering no generalization to new data points. Domain-level methods ( Xie et al., 2023a ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2026 ) partition the training data into domains and assign one data weight to each domain. Chameleon ( Xie et al., 2025 ) and Data Mixing Agent ( Yang et al., 2026 ) further introduce a shared domain taxonomy that enables limited weight sharing among data domains. However, domain-level weights are too coarse to capture the crucial differences in data quality and content within each domain ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Meta-network methods ( Shu et al., 2019 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Calian et al., 2026 ) train a meta-network to output the weight for each data point directly. In theory, this should allow generalization to new data points; in practice, no generalization has been reported. Notably, DataRater ( Calian et al., 2026 ) trains a separate scorer for each dataset, suggesting generalization across dataset is challenging even when the network are trained with a huge amount of data. With this paper, we analyze the reasons behind the challenge mathematically and offer a simple, practical, and high-performance solution. Shortcut Learning. Shortcut learning occurs when models rely on easy features that are strongly predictive of training labels but whose correlations weaken or reverse under distribution shifts, impairing out-of-distribution generalization ( Geirhos et al., 2020 ; Shah et al., 2020 ) . Prior work distinguishes predictivity , how reliably a feature predicts training labels, from availability , how easily it can be extracted ( Hermann et al., 2024 ) . Scimeca et al. (2021) find that solutions favoring easy-to-learn cues tend to lie in flatter minima and are more abundant in parameter space, while Qiu et al. (2024) show that simpler or more strongly correlated spurious features can slow core-feature learning. We investigate these dynamics in data selection networks.
